systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Travail de recherche : utilise EXACTEMENT ces intertitres, dans cet ordre : « La question » (pourquoi ce travail, d'après l'introduction) ; « Les conclusions » (principaux résultats, avec les chiffres) ; « La méthode » (données et démarche, en quelques phrases) ; « Ce que ça implique » (explication accessible des conséquences, telles que les auteurs les présentent) ; « Les limites » (uniquement celles mentionnées par les auteurs ; omets cette section s'ils n'en mentionnent aucune). Remplis « reference » : auteurs, institution ou revue, date, et nature du document (document de travail non relu par des pairs, article de revue à comité de lecture, billet de chercheur…), uniquement d'après le texte fourni.

Date du flux : 19/11/2026
Auteur : James A Watson; Andrea L Conroy; Anthony Batte; Ruth Namazzi; Michael T Hawkes; Kevin C Kain; Katherine Plewes; Stije Leopold; Hugh Kingston; Tran Tinh Hien; Sam Strudwick; Rupert Higgins; Chandy John; Nguyen Hoan Phu; Elizabeth C George; Ann Sarah Walker; Nicholas P J Day; Thomas N Williams; Arjen M Dondorp; Kathryn Maitland; Nicholas J White
Titre d'origine : Acute kidney injury and death in severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria: An individual patient data meta-analysis

ARTICLE :
Figures
Abstract
Background
Serum or plasma concentrations of creatinine and urea are the usual laboratory parameters measured to assess acute kidney injury (AKI) in patients with suspected severe malaria. Creatinine is preferred for estimation of the glomerular filtration rate, but the current threshold for defining severe malaria (>265 μmol/L or a urea >20 mmol/L) is based on adult values and does not reflect the large difference between children and adults in normal values resulting from differences in muscle mass. We reevaluated these thresholds and their prognostic significance in severe malaria using individual patient data from large prospective studies.
Methods and findings
We pooled individual patient data from 22,663 patients recruited into 14 studies of severe malaria of whom 16,441 were included in the primary analysis population. Patients were included in the primary analysis population if their age (if missing, imputed from weight or height), coma status on admission, and either an admission serum or plasma creatinine or urea measurement (blood urea nitrogen, BUN), were all recorded. The primary outcome was mortality by day 28. The secondary outcome was the admission plasma Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein 2 (PfHRP2) concentration (a measure of parasite biomass). Bayesian penalised spline regression models were used to characterise the age-specific relationships (interaction with age) between the outcome and the absolute creatinine, the creatinine fold change relative to the age/weight predicted baseline, and the absolute urea. The models adjusted for coma status and calendar year, with nested random additive effects by study site and study. We estimated threshold plasma or serum creatinine and urea concentrations associated with >5% mortality with probability > 0.9. The majority (84%; 13,793/16,441) were children under 15 years of age. Current thresholds for AKI were associated with mortalities greater than 5%. An admission creatinine greater than three times the age/weight predicted baseline value was associated with >5% mortality. An admission urea >10 mmol/L had approximately similar prognostic value. A urea >10 mmol/L was 3.5 times more common in adults than children. In children <15 years of age, urea was a better prognostic indicator of death than creatinine and, unlike creatinine, correlated with the plasma PfHRP2 concentration. The main limitations of this analysis are the lack of metadata documenting laboratory methods and wide heterogeneity in eligibility criteria, such as creatinine or urea admission values for inclusion.
Conclusions
Admission serum or plasma creatinine >3 times the age/weight predicted baseline value (KDIGO AKI stage 3) can be used to define severe malaria AKI. In children, urea is a better predictor of the true infection biomass and a better prognostic indicator for death. We recommend the following as defining criteria for severe malaria: either a urea (BUN) threshold of 10 mmol/L for both children and adults, or simple age-based thresholds representing approximately >3 times fold change in creatinine from predicted baseline. These updated thresholds identify between 4 and 8 times more children with severe malaria AKI who are at a high risk of death.
Author summary
Why was this study done?
- Acute kidney injury (AKI) has been thought to be rare in children and common in adults, based on the World Health Organization (WHO) definition which is a creatinine >265 μmol/L or a urea >20 mmol/L.
- However, these thresholds were based on data from adult patients. For creatinine, a threshold of 265 μmol/L represents a much greater decrease in glomerular filtration rate due to lower muscle mass (greater fold change from baseline) and so will underestimate the proportion of children with severe malaria AKI.
What did the researchers do and find?
- We pooled individual patient data from 14 prospective studies of severe malaria or severe paediatric disease, where urea or creatinine was measured on admission. This gave a total of more than 16,000 patients, the majority of whom were children.
- We then calibrated thresholds for urea and creatinine by determining values that resulted in more than 5% chance of death. The suggested updated thresholds are >3 times the age or weighted predicted baseline creatinine, or a urea >10 mmol/L.
- Under these revised thresholds, the number of children who would be classified as severe malaria AKI increases by 4- to 8-fold.
What do these findings mean?
- Current criteria substantially under-diagnose severe malaria AKI in children, even though the proportion with severe malaria AKI is lower in children than in adults.
- The WHO definition of severe malaria AKI should be updated. This will ensure children with severe malaria AKI are correctly identified and managed.
- Limitations of this study include lack of documentation of how laboratory measurements were taken, and substantial variation in which populations were eligible for inclusion in the individual studies.

Introduction
Severe malaria is a medical emergency requiring rapid assessment and immediate treatment with artesunate, preferably by the parenteral route [1]. Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria is characterised clinically by vital organ dysfunction usually as a direct consequence of a high parasite biomass and extensive parasitised erythrocyte sequestration. There is no absolute distinction between uncomplicated malaria and severe malaria, but rather a continuum of severity. The most appropriate definition of ‘severe malaria’ depends on the context. A more stringent definition is applied in a research setting compared to the inclusive indicators used in routine clinical care [1]. A general approach for defining severe malaria is to determine sets of clinical signs along with laboratory parameters which indicate an expected mortality greater than some threshold. For example, any clinical presentation with a diagnosis of malaria as the primary cause of illness and >5% chance of death could be categorised as ‘severe malaria’ [2]. That represents a mortality at least 50 times higher than that associated with ‘uncomplicated falciparum malaria’. This risk-based approach rationalises the definition, and allows it to be evidence-based.
Current definitions of severe malaria used by the World Health Organization (WHO) are based on expert consensus on the diagnostic and prognostic value of a range of clinical and laboratory parameters [1]. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is an important manifestation of severe falciparum malaria. It is a common presentation in adults in low transmission settings [3], and for these patients effective renal replacement therapy reduces mortality substantially [4]. Clinically significant AKI was thought to be less common in children with severe malaria in high-transmission settings, although it has long been recognised that elevated biochemical measures of reduced kidney function were associated with increased mortality [5,6]. The AKI thresholds now used as criteria to define severe malaria (a plasma or serum creatinine >265 μmol/L or blood urea nitrogen [BUN] >20 mmol/L) were based on observational studies done in adults. They were not modified for children, in whom muscle mass, and thus baseline plasma or serum creatinine levels, are lower. Recent studies from East Africa indicate that AKI in children hospitalised with malaria is more common than appreciated previously because the current thresholds for determining AKI, based on adult normal values, are too high for children [7,8]. Thus, the current creatinine threshold for severe malaria reflects a much greater reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in children, particularly the youngest children, than it does in adults. It is unclear what these high concentrations represent in terms of expected mortality in children presenting with suspected severe malaria.
We aimed to reevaluate and standardise the AKI thresholds to define severe malaria in adults and children by comparing the prognostic values of specific absolute and relative thresholds of serum creatinine and BUN using a pooled database comprising over 16,000 children and adults recruited into prospective studies of severe malaria. We compared the considered thresholds with the current thresholds for venous lactate concentration (one of the best measures of falciparum malaria disease severity which is independent of AKI [9,10]). The goal of the analysis was to determine optimal thresholds to be used in clinical management to identify both children and adults with suspected severe malaria who are at a substantially elevated risk of death, and characterise how general nephrology consensus criteria for AKI (e.g., KDIGO: https://www.kdigo.org) perform in severe malaria.
Methods
Ethics statement
This meta-analysis uses pseudonymised individual patient data with no identifying variables, so the ethics clearance was waived for the current analysis, as per the Oxford Tropical Research Ethics Committee guidance.
Data
Randomised trials and prospective observational cohort studies enrolling adults or children with suspected severe malaria with at least one baseline BUN (or urea) or creatinine measurement were eligible for inclusion. Studies of children or adults with severe febrile illness not specifically recruiting severe malaria but which had a subset of patients with severe malaria (e.g., the FEAST trial which recruited children with shock and febrile illness [11]) were also eligible for inclusion. Studies were identified from the WHO 2014 review of severe malaria [1], and a systematic review of the literature of all studies done since 2014 (see details of the systematic review in S1 Appendix). For all identified studies, study authors were contacted and asked to upload the data to the secure Infectious Diseases Data Observatory (IDDO) data platform. All data were then curated to a standardised CDISC SDTM format prior to analysis. Extensive data checking was carried out before pooling of data. A prospective protocol was not pre-registered before data analysis. A high-level analysis plan was drafted as part of the data request (S2 Appendix). The analyses were conducted according to PRISMA-IPD guidelines, apart from risk of bias assessments which were not relevant for this meta-analysis (S1 Checklist).
Analysis population
The primary analysis population consisted of patients in the pooled database who had all of the following recorded:
- A confirmed malaria infection at admission/enrolment (microscopy or rapid diagnostic test);
- Age either directly recorded or imputed from weight or height;
- Coma status at presentation;
- Mortality outcome at hospital discharge or by day 28 after admission;
- Admission plasma or serum creatinine or BUN measurement.
Outcomes and exposure definitions
The primary outcome was within-hospital mortality up to day 28. Many of the older studies did not systematically record the time to death, and so we use a binary outcome of died versus survived. The secondary outcome was the plasma Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein 2 (PfHRP2) concentration: this was chosen because it is a proxy measurement of the parasite biomass and thus the severity of the falciparum malaria infection [12,13].
Three exposure variables were defined: (i) the admission BUN; (ii) the admission creatinine; and the (iii) admission fold change in creatinine from the predicted baseline normal value. All analyses used log-transformed creatinine or BUN because the values are approximately log-normally distributed. The primary exposure-outcome analyses were performed on the complete-case datasets: all patients who had a measured BUN or creatinine, respectively. This is because missingness of BUN or creatinine measurements was almost entirely due to individual studies not taking these measurements (S1 Fig). We use molar BUN concentrations which are the same as molar urea concentrations (whereas in mg/dL the blood urea is 2.14 times the BUN concentration).
Statistical analysis
Regression modelling. All regression models included coma (yes/no; Glasgow Coma score <11 in adults, Blantyre Coma score <3 in children) as an independent predictor of outcome as this was recorded systematically across all studies and it is the strongest predictor of death. We did not include other clinical or laboratory variables as these were not consistently recorded, and we were primarily interested in the univariate relationship between the exposure (creatinine or BUN) and death. All regression models estimated age-dependent relationships between the exposure variables and death (interaction term between age as a continuous variable and the exposure variable), modelled using a tensor-product smooth between the exposure variable and age with cubic regression splines. We also explored models that categorised age divided into three categories: < 5, [5,15), and ≥15 years. Nested random intercepts were specified for each study and study site. All models included a temporal spline for calendar year as there have been substantial improvements in treatment and supportive care over the 40-year period over which these studies were conducted; hence, time could plausibly confound the relationship between exposure values and the outcome.
For the analysis comparing the prognostic value of BUN versus creatinine, we included only the subset of patients who had both values recorded at baseline. For the comparative analysis examining the relationship between plasma lactate and mortality, we included only patients in the primary analysis population who also had a recorded baseline hemoglobin or hematocrit measurement. An interaction term was included for hemoglobin above 5 g/dL. If hemoglobin was missing, but the hematocrit was recorded, the hemoglobin was imputed using a 1/3 transformation from hematocrit (%) to hemoglobin (g/dL), S2 Fig [14].
For the creatinine analysis, we compared the absolute creatinine values (μmol/L) and the creatinine fold change relative to a predicted age- and weight-adjusted normal baseline value. As pre-illness baseline creatinine was not available for any patients, it was estimated. To estimate the normal baseline values in children under 15 years, we compared two separate approaches: the Pottel equation which is based on age only (baseline Cr (0.244 / 120) [15]; and the Schwartz equation which is based on height only (15]. We then compared the predicted baseline creatinine values with the observed recovery values in a subset of patients recruited into the TRACT trial in Malawi who had follow-up creatinine and BUN both measured at 28, 90 and 180 days post-admission (n = 404 patients with ages ranging from 2 months to 12 years). This assumes the later measurements were equivalent to baseline values. The normal baseline values for patients over 15 years of age were estimated using the well-established Cockcroft–Gault equation, assuming a normal creatinine clearance of 120 mL/min. This equation was chosen as it incorporates both age and weight. The primary analysis used the age- and weight-based predicted baseline values (Pottel equation for children and Cockcroft-Gault equation for adults) because age was missing in only 6 patients and weight was missing in only 5% of patients. A sensitivity analysis explored compared the results when using the Schwartz equation (based on height) for the predicted baseline creatinine.
Single imputation of age, weight and height. To calculate creatinine fold change in all patients with measured creatinine values at baseline using age, weight or height, we performed single imputation using chained equations for age, weight, height, mid-upper arm circumference and the key laboratory parameters (lactate, creatinine, BUN, bicarbonate, hemoglobin). The single imputation included the mortality outcome, sex, study and study site. We used random forests for the multiple imputation model as it allows for non-linear relationships between variables (notably relationship between age, weight and height is non-linear). Visual checks of the imputed versus complete case bivariate distributions were carried out to check the imputation outputs (S3 Fig). Single imputation was used because age was missing in only 6 patients in the creatinine analysis dataset; and weight was only missing in 503 patients (5%) in the creatinine analysis dataset. Height was missing in 2,134 patients (22%). Standardised differences and Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) statistic were used to compare imputed with observed data, stratified by age (S3 Table).
Threshold estimation. In order to have comparable thresholds across different laboratory measurements, we estimated approximate values at which expected mortality was above 5%. This used the posterior predictive distribution of mortality outcomes from each Bayesian regression model, ignoring random effect terms (values set to zero). Thresholds were then chosen as values for which approximately 90% of the posterior mass was above 5% (function posterior_epred).
Changes to the planned analysis. Relative to the initial analysis plan, the primary exposure-outcome analyses were restricted to complete cases rather than imputed data, because missingness of creatinine and urea was almost entirely determined at the study level rather than at the patient level, so that imputation would have required imputing an entire study’s values (S1 Fig). In response to peer review, we added an analysis of random-effect variance components with median odds ratios (S1 Table; S18 and S19 Figs), quantitative imputation diagnostics (S3 Table) and receiver operating characteristic curves (S11 Fig); these are additional reporting of the planned analysis and did not change any estimates. The analyses of hyperkalaemia, acidosis and the relationship with plasma PfHRP2 were exploratory and data-driven, prompted by unexpected patterns in the pooled data.
Software. Bayesian generalised linear models with penalised spline terms were fitted for in-hospital mortality (Bernoulli likelihood, logit link) using the brms package which constructs the spline bases via mgcv and uses stan to estimate posterior distributions [16–18]. Each smooth term is decomposed into an unpenalised component (population-level coefficient), and one or more penalised components whose basis coefficients are given zero-mean Gaussian priors each with its own standard deviation
The primary analysis models used a tensor-product smooth (t2) between the exposure and age constructed from two marginal cubic regression spline bases of dimension five, giving 24 basis coefficients and three separate penalties (one for each marginal main effect and one for their interaction). The calendar-year smooth used a thin-plate regression spline basis of dimension 10. The supporting models in which age was divided into three categories used a univariate cubic regression spline basis of dimension 10 for the exposure, together with a factor-smooth interaction (bs = “fs", k = 10, m = 1) that penalises the deviation of each age group’s curve from the common curve. Basis dimensions set an upper bound on flexibility; the estimated curvature is determined by the posterior distribution of PfHRP2 outcome using lme4 (maximum likelihood estimation) [19].
We used the brms default priors, which were not modified. The prior on the standard deviation parameters (smoothing standard deviations of every spline term and the standard deviations of the nested study and study-site random intercepts) and the intercept were Student-t(3, 0, 2.5) (three degrees of freedom, location zero and scale 2.5, truncated at zero for standard deviation parameters). The remaining population-level coefficients (coma status and the unpenalised components of the smooths) were given improper flat priors. This shrinkage controlled model complexity; no additional variable selection or tuning of penalties was carried out. The number of observations was large relative to the number of basis coefficients. Between-study and between-site heterogeneity in mortality risk was summarised for all fitted models by the posterior standard deviations of the random effects and by the corresponding median odds ratios (S1 Table) [20], with the estimated study- and site-level random effects shown in S18 and S19 Figs. To compare the effects of creatinine and urea exposure effects against each other and against the across-study and site variance, a multivariable model was fitted with both exposures standardised (zero mean and unit variance).
All Bayesian models were fitted using four chains of 2,000 iterations, of which the first 1,000 were discarded as warmup. Convergence was satisfactory for all reported models (PfHRP2 outcome using lme4 (maximum likelihood estimation) [19]. Imputation using chained equations with random forests used the mice package [21]. Euler diagrams (generalisation of Venn diagrams to up to 5 categories) were estimated from imputed data (BUN, hemoglobin, lactate) using the R package eulerr [22]. Detailed model fits and parameter estimates are given in the accompanying github repository.
Results
Participants
Individual patient data from 14 studies were pooled, providing data from a total of 22,663 patients. After excluding one study with unreliable creatinine measurements and one study that had no urea or creatinine data, 16,441 patients from 12 studies had a recorded or imputed age, coma status, parasitological confirmation of malaria at baseline, a recorded mortality outcome, and at least one baseline measurement of creatinine or urea (BUN). These 16,441 patients were included in the analysis population (9,848 patients had creatinine measured on admission; 12,537 patients had urea (BUN) measured on admission; and 5,944 patients had both), S4 Fig. Table 1 shows the demographic characteristics of the patients in the analysis population stratified by study. The majority of patients were children (n = 13,793 <15 years, 84%) and from Africa (n = 13,533, 82%). 9.5% of all patients died within 28 days of admission (n = 1,569/16,441).
Age and weight dependent distribution of creatinine and urea in severe malaria patients
Fig 1 shows the relationship between weight (kg, square root scale) or age (years, square root scale) and the admission serum or plasma creatinine (left panels) and urea (right panels; both on the log10 scale). For both creatinine and urea there was, as expected, a clear relationship between weight/age and admission values, with substantial inter-individual variation. When comparing children (defined as patients younger than 15 years of age) versus adults (≥15 years), the median serum or plasma creatinine values were 45 µmol/L (interquartile range [IQR]: 31, 64) versus 155 µmol/L (IQR: 113, 256), respectively; i.e., they were approximately 3.4 times higher in adults. For urea the median values were 4.6 mmol/L (IQR: 2.9, 7.5) versus 10.9 mmol/L (IQR: 6.4, 21.4), i.e., approximately 2.4 times higher in adults. The larger difference between creatinine values in adults versus children likely reflects the stronger dependence of creatinine on muscle mass and hence weight/age. This was also reflected by a systematic difference in the creatinine/urea ratios between children and adults (Fig 2). The relationship between weight and urea was consistent across five large studies [11,26,28,30,31] which all used the portable i-STAT machine (Abbott) to measure BUN (S5 Fig).

In children under 15 years of age, only 2.4% had a plasma or serum creatinine above 265 µmol/L (n = 205/8,473); whereas in older children and adults, 24.4% had a creatinine above 265 µmol/L (336/1,375). For urea, 4.5% of patients younger than 15 years of age had an admission value above the current threshold of 20 mmol/L (n = 463/10,248), versus 27.2% for patients older than 15 years (n = 622/2,289). The aggregate day 28 case fatality ratios were 8.1% in children younger than 15 years (n = 1,116/13,793) and 17.1% in those older than 15 years (n = 453/2,648).
Prognostic value of creatinine and BUN
To explore the relationships between creatinine, urea and mortality by day 28 we divided patients into four categories for renal biomarkers (creatinine: ≤65, (65, 130], (130, 265], >265 µmol/L; urea: ≤5, (5, 10], (10, 20], >20 mmol/L). As coma on admission has the greatest prognostic significance of all clinical variables, we estimated the proportion of patients who died in each creatinine and urea category, subdivided by coma status on admission (yes/no) and age (<15 years versus ≥15 years). Only 119 out of 6,553 children under 5 years of age with a measured creatinine had values above 265 μmol/L, nearly all of whom were from the TRACT study (83%) with corresponding low mortality by day 28. Apart from this group, in patients meeting the current WHO AKI threshold for defining severe malaria (plasma or serum creatinine >265 μmol/L or urea >20 mmol/L), the observed mortality was 5% or more in both children and adults, even without coma on admission (Fig 3). Mortality was greater than 5% for threshold values of 130 μmol/L for creatinine and 10 mmol/L for urea (i.e., half the current thresholds).

There was clear heterogeneity between the absolute plasma or serum creatinine value and mean case fatality ratio by age (Fig 3). The same absolute creatinine thresholds implied substantially different expected mortalities in children versus adults. This was less apparent for urea. In order to harmonise comparisons between adults and children, we estimated a creatinine fold change from predicted baseline values and used that as the primary exposure variable. Using 6-month follow-up data from children in Malawi recruited into the TRACT trial to provide normal paediatric baseline values, there was a clear linear relationship between age and baseline creatinine, the slope of which was well approximated by the Schwartz equation (it had a systematic upwards bias, but the residuals were less correlated with the baseline value relative to the Pottel equation, Figs 4 and S6). Height, age and weight all had approximately the same predictive value (explaining roughly 50% of the variance in baseline creatinine values in these data). As expected, urea did not vary by age or weight, apart from in the youngest children (<2 years), Fig 4. Very young children (under 1 year of age) had baseline urea concentration around 30% lower than the older children (approximately 2.0 mmol/L versus 2.85 mmol/L).
n = 404 had post-illness creatinines and n = 361 had post-illness urea. The blue lines show spline fits and the red lines show either the Schwartz equation prediction (height vs. creatinine) or the Pottel equation prediction (age vs. creatinine).
As expected, given the large variation in baseline creatinine by age, there was considerable variation in predicted mortality as a function of the absolute creatinine values by age (Figs 5 and S7). In patients without coma, the probability of >5% mortality exceeded 90% for a creatinine around 80 μmol/L in children, compared with around 200 μmol/L in adults. However, under the same model structure, there was very little residual heterogeneity by age in the predicted mortality relationship when using the creatinine fold change based on the Pottel equation for children and the Cockcroft-Gault equation for adults. There was also no clear age heterogeneity in children when using the Schwartz equation (S8 Fig). A three times increase in predicted baseline creatinine (i.e., KDIGO AKI stage 3) was associated with a mortality >5% in all age groups (Fig 5). This was lower for the Schwartz equation which predicted higher baseline values. For urea, there was considerably less heterogeneity between the absolute value and the predicted risk of death. Older children and adults had slightly higher threshold values (between 12 and 14 mmol/L) associated with >0.9 probability that death would occur in >5% of patients, Fig 5. There was no clear relationship with mortality outcomes (S16 Fig).

In a multivariable logistic regression model comparing creatinine fold change and urea (BUN) (both on the log2 scale), with an interaction by age category, adjusted for coma status, a doubling in admission urea was a better predictor of death than a doubling in admission creatinine fold change in all age groups under 15 years. In adults urea and creatinine had similar prognostic value (S9-S11 Figs). A doubling in plasma or serum creatinine relative to the age/weight predicted baseline was associated with an adjusted odds ratio for death of 1.91 (95% credible interval [CrI]: 1.39, 2.62) in patients >15 years, whereas for all age groups in children under 15 years the CrI included 1. In comparison, a doubling of urea was associated with an increased risk of death in all age groups with estimated odds ratio between 1.2 (95% CrI: 1.02, 1.81; >15 years) and 2.09 (95% CrI: 1.39, 3.17; children between 5 and 15 years). Overall, creatinine fold change, BUN and lactate had similar prognostic values for death by day 28 with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of approximately 0.72 (S11 Fig). However, this masked important heterogeneity between adults and children. In children, both the urea and creatinine thresholds had low sensitivity (50% or lower) but high specificity for death; in adults the sensitivity was much higher (82% for urea >10 mmol/L), but the specificity was only 50% (Table 2). In comparison, a lactate threshold of 5 mmol/L had similar sensitivities (∼65%) and specificities (∼75%) in all age groups. Residual heterogeneity in baseline mortality risk between studies and sites (nested random effects) was consistent across all model parameterisations (S1 Table) and approximately the same order of magnitude of effect as one standard deviation change in the log10 urea or the log2 creatinine fold change (S2 Table).
Hyperkalemia in severe malaria
Hyperkalemia is associated with both AKI and acidosis (of any cause). Clinically significant hyperkalemia (K+ > 6.5 mmol/L) on admission was recorded in 3.9% (583/14,952) of patients with admission potassium values. Nearly all were in children (only 19 out of 2,377 [0.8%] were in adults). Elevated creatinine or urea concentrations were only weakly predictive of hyperkalemia (Fig 6) with a large number of children with hyperkalemia and BUN <10 mmol/L. Very low bicarbonate (<10 mEq/L) was the strongest predictor of hyperkalemia.

Association of AKI with parasite biomass
In the pooled database, there were 4,116 patients from 4 studies with admission plasma PfHRP2 and creatinine both measured, and 7,697 patients from 5 studies with admission plasma PfHRP2 and BUN both measured. All were children under 15 years of age. Plasma PfHRP2 is the best quantitative marker of the total parasite biomass and thus the true underlying severity of the infection [12]. We assessed its relationship with admission creatinine fold change and urea. In the TRACT trial, there was a large subgroup of patients with very low plasma PfHRP2 and high creatinine and high BUN with an unexpectedly low case fatality ratio (S12 and S13 Figs). The reason for this was unclear. In patients with a plasma PfHRP2 > 1,000 ng/ml (i.e., patients likely to have true severe malaria [13]), there was little correlation between plasma PfHRP2 and creatinine fold change, but there was a strong correlation between plasma PfHRP2 and BUN (S14 Fig).
Attributable fraction of AKI in children and adults
We used the full analysis dataset with multiple imputation for missing data to estimate the proportion of patients with a presentation of reduced kidney function (urea >10 mmol/L), versus cerebral malaria, severe anaemia (hemoglobin <5 g/dL), and lactic acidosis (lactate ≥5 mmol/L). Seventy-five percent of patients in the analysis dataset (12,253/16,441) met one of these categories (10,134/13,793 children and 2,119/2,648 adults). Fig 7 shows the estimated individual proportions and overlaps for each category. A urea >10 mmol/L was a dominant manifestation in adults (54%), but only occurred in 16% of children (i.e., 3.5 times more common in adults). Very high urea concentrations (>30 mmol/L) occurred in approximately 3.5% of children and 15% of adults (i.e., 4 times more common in adults). Analysis of the complete case data gave very similar proportions.

Discussion
Severe falciparum malaria is a multi-system disease and a major cause of death in endemic areas. Identifying patients with severe malaria is essential for appropriate triage, and also for the correct evaluation of therapies. The current definition of severe malaria used in clinical research comprises a list of clinical or laboratory abnormalities, any one of which fulfils the definition. All, except the anaemia criterion (hemoglobin less than 5 g/dL), are associated with a mortality >5% [2]. AKI is an important manifestation of severe malaria, but the biochemical thresholds used to define it have not been calibrated to a mortality threshold of 5%, and have been based on values three times the upper limit of normal in adults, whereas most deaths from severe falciparum malaria occur in children. The degree of reduced kidney function is usually assessed from a plasma or serum measurement of creatinine or urea. Plasma or serum creatinine is more accurate than urea as an indirect measure of the GFR but, as the level depends on the muscle mass, values in children are much lower than those in adults, particularly if they are malnourished [34]. Creatinine levels should therefore be adjusted for lean body mass to provide comparable estimates of GFR. As a consequence, the current severe malaria threshold (>265 μmol/L) is an insensitive indicator in children.
This individual patient meta-analysis confirms that the admission fold-change in plasma or serum creatinine (above the predicted normal value) is highly predictive of death and that a 3-fold increase is generally associated with a mortality above 5%. This corresponds to a KDIGO AKI stage 3 classification [35]. Using age or weight adjustment, the normal values are satisfactorily predicted by widely used equations (e.g., the Pottel equation, Fig 4). These age/weight corrections removed nearly all the observed heterogeneity across age groups between creatinine and mortality outcomes. Simple age-based thresholds suitable for African children have been proposed [8]. We recommend a simple set of approximate thresholds for identifying children and adults at elevated risk of death (S15 Fig). As expected, creatinine and urea levels were strongly correlated, but urea is a better prognosticator of death, likely because it is a better overall severity marker. In addition, other sources of variability such as malnutrition influence the creatinine level more than the BUN. In severe malaria, increased metabolism and variable dehydration both contribute to the rise in urea. However, the urea concentration (often reported as BUN) was a better prognosticator than the creatinine concentration in children. In addition, apart from in very young children, urea was not strongly determined by weight or age (Fig 4) and, unlike creatinine, there was not large age-based heterogeneity in its predictive value.
